records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2003 states that the transition from roughly human-level artificial intelligence to full superintelligence may be very rapid, perhaps a matter of days rather than years, and names this possibility the singularity hypothesis.

attested.note: The wording is read in the undated revised version on the author's site; the 2003 printed wording was not compared, so the date from which it is attested is unknown.

records.qualification: A statement of possibility ('may'), not a forecast with a probability, and not evidence that such a transition will occur. Read in the current web expression, which may have been revised after 2003. Earlier texts on the overlapping dataset concept A4 (Yudkowsky, Creating Friendly AI, 2001; AI as a Positive and Negative Factor in Global Risk, 2006) are linked, not re-recorded.

evidence.locator: Section 2, "Superintelligence Is Different", paragraph on the final stage of the transition
evidence.passage: the transition from a state where we have a roughly human-level artificial intelligence to a state where we have full-blown superintelligence, with revolutionary applications, may be very rapid, perhaps a matter of days rather than years

records.statement: Chalmers's paper of 2010 sets out the argument that, once there is AI of greater than human intelligence, an intelligence explosion will follow to AI far beyond human level, and states that 'within years' would not be an unreasonable timeframe for that step, while stipulating 'within decades' as the conservative reading.
records.missing: A short period: the paper suggests “within years” for the step to AI++ and takes “within decades” as its conservative reading; “within days” is reported as what some would suggest.
records.qualification: Chalmers analyses the argument and its premises, qualifies each step with 'absent defeaters', and adopts 'within decades' as the conservative timeframe; the record does not show that he predicts a transition of hours to months. The term qualifies the record through the usual name 'intelligence explosion', which he attributes to Good (1965). The dataset already records the paper's discussion of the concept (lineage-chalmers-discusses-explosion), not a stance on it.

evidence.passage: One view is that this event will be followed by an explosion to ever-greater levels of intelligence, as each generation of machines creates more intelligent machines in turn.

I think it would not be unreasonable to suggest “within years” here (and some would suggest “within days” or even sooner for the second step), but as before “within decades” is conservative while still being interesting.

records.statement: Muehlhauser and Salamon's chapter of 2012 states that human-level AI may be followed, fairly rapidly, by an intelligence explosion to systems whose capabilities far surpass those of humanity as a whole, and argues that there is a good chance of this if human-level AI is created.
records.missing: A short period or a fast-takeoff name: the chapter says the explosion follows “fairly rapidly”, without a period.
records.qualification: Read in MIRI's PDF, which states that it contains changes from the Springer chapter. 'Fairly rapidly' names no period; the record rests on the chapter's use of the name 'intelligence explosion' for the transition. A statement of the authors' argument, not evidence that it is correct.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 2, Section 1, Introduction, first paragraph
evidence.passage: Shortly thereafter, we may see an “intelligence explosion” or “technological singularity”—a chain of events by which human-level AI leads, fairly rapidly, to intelligent systems whose capabilities far surpass those of biological humanity as a whole.
if human-level AI is created, there is a good chance vastly superhuman AI will follow via an “intelligence explosion,”

records.statement: Yudkowsky's post of 20 October 2017 states that AlphaGo Zero's progress to a strongly superhuman level at Go, after three days of self-play within about two years of a time when no program had come close to beating a professional, is evidence for his side of the AI-foom debate with Hanson, and that fast capability gains resembling foom need not require self-improvement.
records.qualification: The post treats a narrow, closed domain (Go) as evidence about general capability gains and says so ('AlphaGo clearly isn't a general AI'). It holds the earliest-located role only through its use of the name “foom” for the transition, not through a stated period (the Go comparison spans two years, and the three days are of self-play in Go). It is the author's reading of one result, not a measurement of general takeoff speed. Texts by Yudkowsky already recorded on A4 (Hard Takeoff, 2008; Intelligence Explosion Microeconomics, 2013) are linked.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "Sheer speed of capability gain"
evidence.passage: Go play went from “nobody has come close to winning against a professional” to “so strongly superhuman they’re not really bothering any more” over two years … says you don’t even need self-improvement to get things that look like FOOM.

records.statement: Yudkowsky's post of 20 October 2017 argues that AlphaGo Zero's discarding of accumulated human Go knowledge counts against Hanson's thesis that cumulative domain knowledge and a market ecology of components would prevent rapid gains in AI capability across domains.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that accumulated domain knowledge and an ecology of specialised components keep capability gains slow and distributed.

records.qualification: The post contests Hanson's position as Yudkowsky states it ('as I understand the Hansonian thesis'); Hanson's own texts are recorded separately. Evidence from one closed domain.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "I emphasize how all the mighty human edifice of Go knowledge"
evidence.passage: These mighty edifices of human knowledge, as I understand the Hansonian thesis, are supposed to be the bulwark against rapid gains in AI capability across multiple domains at once.

records.statement: Hanson's post of 24 July 2014 argues that a 'local explosion', in which one small project's machine goes within weeks from weaker than a human to able to take over the world, is implausible, because one project could not innovate across thousands of software modules vastly faster than the rest of the world.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that one small project could improve software across the full range of mental modules faster than the rest of the world.

records.qualification: The post contests the single-project, weeks-long form of the proposition; it accepts that machines may eventually do most mental tasks better and may greatly raise economic growth rates. Hanson's earlier posts in the debate with Yudkowsky (2008–2013) are in the dataset and are linked, not re-recorded; this is the earliest located contesting record within the pack's own searches, not before them.

evidence.passage: a single machine, built by a single project using only a tiny fraction of world resources, goes in a short time (e.g., weeks) from being so weak that it is usually beat by a single human … to so powerful that it easily takes over the entire world.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "Similarly, while you might imagine"
evidence.passage: So I can’t see a plausible way one project could increase its intelligence vastly faster than could the rest of the world.

records.statement: Hanson's post of 6 May 2022 states that recent large AI systems, with simple separate values and almost no self-reflection or self-improvement, offer little support for the scenario in which one system 'fooms' over days to weeks, and that he still finds foom unlikely though not impossible.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that capability gains will come through self-reflection and self-modification of one system.

records.qualification: Hanson describes the scenario he contests in his own words and states that he regards the evidence from recent systems as weak.

evidence.passage: recent developments offer little support for the hypothesis that AAGI will be created soon via the process of self-reflection and self-improvement
I’m not saying foom is impossible, just that it looks unlikely

records.statement: Walsh's paper of February 2016 argues that there will not be the runaway exponential growth of a technological singularity, giving arguments that include diminishing returns to self-improvement, while predicting superhuman AI within 30 or 40 years.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that each generation of self-improvement yields a constant or growing improvement.

records.qualification: Walsh contests runaway growth, not superhuman AI as such; the paper states that he expects super-human intelligence in 30 to 40 years.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 2, section "Some arguments against the Singularity"
evidence.passage: I am not predicting that AI will fail to achieve super-human intelligence. Like many of my colleagues working in AI, I predict we are just 30 or 40 years away from this event. However, I am suggesting that there will not be the run away exponential growth predicted by some.
if each generation only improves by half the last change, then the system will never get beyond doubling its overall intelligence.

records.statement: Benthall's paper of February 2017 argues, using a Bayesian model of a reasoning agent, that there are important limits to how far an agent can improve its predictive ability through self-modification alone, and so rejects the scenario of rapid self-improvement to superintelligence.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that an agent can rapidly raise its predictive ability by self-modification (the recalcitrance of prediction).

records.qualification: A model-based argument about one capacity (prediction) that the author holds the scenario depends on; it addresses Bostrom's Superintelligence (2014), which is not retrievable here.

evidence.passage: We argue that this scenario depends on an agent’s ability to rapidly improve its ability to predict its environment through self-modification. Using a Bayesian model of a reasoning agent, we show that there are important limitations to how an agent may improve its predictive ability through self-modification alone.

records.statement: Kelly's essay of April 2017 argues that there is no evidence that intelligence is increasing exponentially and that an imagined intelligence explosion should be pictured not as a cascading boom but as a scattering of new varieties, with experiments and the external world limiting the pace of discovery.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premises that intelligence grows exponentially on a single dimension and that thinking alone, without experiment, yields rapid progress.

records.qualification: Read in the author's blog copy; the Wired version of April 2017 was not compared. Kelly states that a singularity is 'greater than zero' in probability but 'highly unlikely'.

evidence.locator: Section 2 of the five assumptions, on exponential growth
evidence.passage: Therefore when we imagine an “intelligence explosion,” we should imagine it not as a cascading boom but rather as a scattering exfoliation of new varieties.
There won’t be instant discoveries the minute, hour, day or year a so-called “smarter-than-human” AI appears.

records.statement: Brooks's essay of September 2017 argues that abundant computing power does not mean programs are close to doing AI research and rewriting their own code, and describes belief in the singularity as resting on exponentialism.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that programs able to do AI research and improve their own code are near.

records.qualification: Brooks also characterises belief in the singularity as resembling religious belief; the record rests on his argument about self-improving programs, not on that characterisation.

evidence.locator: Section "B. The Singularity", in the discussion of prediction types
evidence.passage: Even if there is a lot of computer power around it does not mean we are close to having programs that can do research in Artificial Intelligence, and rewrite their own code to get better and better.

records.statement: Brooks's essay of September 2017 states that, if superintelligent devices are eventually built, they will evolve technologically over time in a world already changed and populated by many other intelligences, so that their existence will not come as a sudden surprise.
records.qualification: Stated in the section 'Hollywood scenarios'; Brooks names no timescale beyond 'over time'. Yudkowsky's texts recorded on the overlapping dataset concept Y11 (from 2000) are contesting or context records only, so they do not precede this articulation.

evidence.passage: We will not suddenly be surprised by the existence of such super intelligences. They will evolve technologically over time, and our world will be different, populated by many other intelligences, and we will have lots of experience already.

records.statement: AI Impacts' page of February 2018 states that it is not convinced by any argument it has seen for expecting a large discontinuity in AI progress around AGI above the very low base rate for technologies, and argues that positive feedback loops, such as AI improving AI, rarely move fast enough and far enough to dominate.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that a feedback loop of AI improving AI would be exceptionally fast, and the base rate of large technological discontinuities.

records.qualification: The page calls the question open and lists conditions under which it would find the intelligence-explosion argument compelling. Read in the current page, modified 2020-05-26.

evidence.locator: Summary at the head of the page
evidence.passage: We aren’t convinced by any of the arguments we’ve seen to expect large discontinuity in AI progress above the extremely low base rate for all technologies.
Positive feedback loops are common in the world, and very rarely move fast enough and far enough to become a dominant dynamic in the world.

records.statement: Grace's post of 2022 argues that identifying a feedback loop of AI improving AI does not show that the loop is fast, and states that she knows of no strong reason to expect very fast growth in AI capabilities at around human-level performance.

claimed.note: Date in the byline; the post was published on 14 October 2022.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the inference from the existence of a feedback loop to a fast one.

records.qualification: The post presents itself as arguments run past readers ('not an exhaustive literature review') and notes that strong arguments for fast growth might exist.

evidence.locator: Section "Speed of intelligence growth is ambiguous", counterargument to the feedback-loop argument
evidence.passage: Identifying a feedback loop empirically does not signify an explosion of whatever you are looking at.

evidence.locator: Section "Speed of intelligence growth is ambiguous", closing paragraph
evidence.passage: Overall, I don’t know of strong reason to expect very fast growth in AI capabilities at around human-level AI performance, though I hear such arguments might exist.

records.statement: Thorstad's working paper of November 2022 argues that the singularity hypothesis, on which self-improving agents quickly become orders of magnitude more intelligent than humans, rests on implausible growth assumptions, and that the defences by Chalmers (2010) and Bostrom (2014) do not overcome the case against it.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the growth assumptions on which rapid self-improvement to superintelligence depends.

records.qualification: Read in the GPI working-paper expression. 'Most developed' marks the most extended argument against the proposition among the contesting texts located, an editorial judgement.

evidence.passage: In this paper, I argue that the singularity hypothesis rests on implausible growth assumptions. I show how leading philosophical defenses of the singularity hypothesis (Chalmers 2010, Bostrom 2014) fail to overcome the case for skepticism.

records.statement: Narayanan and Kapoor's essay of April 2025 states that the authors reject 'fast takeoff' scenarios and holds that a gradual increase in automation of AI development is more likely than a discontinuous moment of recursive self-improvement.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that recursive self-improvement would arrive as a discontinuous moment, given that AI development already relies on AI.

records.qualification: The essay states a worldview and says so; its argument is mainly about the speed of adoption and diffusion, with a separate argument about the speed of AI methods.

evidence.locator: Introduction, paragraph on the scope of the essay
evidence.passage: Since we reject “fast takeoff” scenarios, we do not see it as necessary or useful to envision a world further ahead than we have attempted to.

evidence.locator: Part I, section "The External world puts a speed limit on AI innovation", paragraph on AI-conducted AI research
evidence.passage: But note that AI development already relies heavily on AI. It is more likely that we will continue to see a gradual increase in the role of automation in AI development than a singular, discontinuous moment when recursive self-improvement is achieved.

records.statement: Narayanan and Kapoor's essay of April 2025 states that a continued gradual increase in the role of automation in AI development is more likely than a singular, discontinuous moment when recursive self-improvement is achieved, and that speed limits apply at each stage from invention to diffusion.
records.qualification: Much of the essay concerns the slowness of economic and societal impact (on the timescale of decades), which is distinct from the speed of capability gains; the record rests on its passage about AI methods.

evidence.locator: Part I, section "The External world puts a speed limit on AI innovation", paragraph on AI-conducted AI research
evidence.passage: It is more likely that we will continue to see a gradual increase in the role of automation in AI development than a singular, discontinuous moment when recursive self-improvement is achieved.

records.statement: Christiano's post of February 2018 states that he thinks a slow takeoff, a continuous acceleration distributed across the economy, significantly more likely than a fast one, arguing that before there is an incredibly intelligent AI there will probably be a slightly worse one.
records.qualification: Christiano's 'slow takeoff' is operationalised as a four-year doubling of world output before a one-year doubling, which is fast by historical standards; the same post states that an intelligence explosion seems very likely to him. The dataset records the post as contesting A4 and articulating A1; this record sits beside those and is not a re-recording of them.

evidence.passage: I currently think a slow takeoff is significantly more likely.
Before we have an incredibly intelligent AI, we will probably have a slightly worse AI.

records.statement: Drexler's report of 2019 states that AI-enabled development of AI could lead to an accelerating feedback process, an intelligence explosion, which he calls a general and plausible concept, and argues that its most direct path runs through distributed automation of AI research and development rather than through a self-transforming AI agent.
records.qualification: Drexler's model separates the intelligence explosion from agency and argues that this path may be more controllable; it states no period for the transition. Read in a third-party copy of the FHI report.

evidence.passage: AI-enabled development of improved AI algorithms could potentially lead to an accelerating feedback process, enabling a so-called “intelligence explosion”. This quite general and plausible concept has commonly been identified with a specific, challenging, and risky implementation
paths to extremely rapid progress in AI technology may be both more direct and more controllable than has been commonly assumed.

records.statement: Aschenbrenner's essay of 2024 states that hundreds of millions of AGIs could automate AI research and compress a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less, so that AI would rapidly go from human-level to vastly superhuman, and names this an intelligence explosion.
records.qualification: A forecast argued from trend extrapolation; the chapter discusses possible bottlenecks and states that none seems sufficient to slow the process decisively. Not evidence that the forecast is correct.

evidence.passage: Hundreds of millions of AGIs could automate AI research, compressing a decade of algorithmic progress (5+ OOMs) into ≤1 year. We would rapidly go from human-level to vastly superhuman AI systems.

records.statement: Aschenbrenner's essay of 2024 argues against the view that deep learning is hitting a wall, holding that trends in compute, algorithmic efficiency and 'unhobbling' make AGI by 2027 'strikingly plausible', and treats the data wall as a source of variance rather than a limit.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premises that scaling trends have stalled and that the shortage of internet data will stop progress short of AGI.

records.qualification: The chapter states that without new methods the pretraining paradigm 'will (at least naively) run out' and that 'we’d plateau'; it argues that labs' research bets are likely to get around this. A forecast, not a demonstration.

evidence.passage: AGI by 2027 is strikingly plausible.
leading some to proclaim stagnation and that deep learning is hitting a wall.1 But by counting the OOMs, we get a peek at what we should actually expect.

records.statement: Kokotajlo, Alexander, Larsen, Lifland and Dean's scenario of April 2025 describes AI systems coming to dominate AI research during 2027 and calls the result an intelligence explosion; its authors state that superintelligence could plausibly arrive by the end of the decade.
records.qualification: A forecast written as a dated scenario, which the authors describe as partly guesswork; the passages in the scenario's narrative are the authors' forecast, not reports of events. The record does not show what any author holds beyond the text.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 17, "August 2027: The Geopolitics of Superintelligence"
evidence.passage: The reality of the intelligence explosion hits the White House. When AI was only giving a 2x or 3x research speedup, it was easy to dismiss as the equivalent of hiring good personal assistants. Now it’s more obvious that AIs are themselves dominating AI research.
we also think it is strikingly plausible that superintelligence could arrive by the end of the decade.

records.statement: Eth and Davidson's paper of March 2025 argues, from a model of technological progress calibrated on recent AI software progress, that once AI fully automates AI research the feedback loop of AI improving AI software would overcome diminishing returns and produce a software intelligence explosion.
records.qualification: A model-based argument whose conclusion depends on estimated returns to software research; the paper discusses bottlenecks such as compute for experiments and training time. Not evidence that the event will occur.

evidence.locator: Summary, paragraph on the model and its calibration
evidence.passage: In our model, this finding implies that the positive feedback loop of AI improving AI software is powerful enough to overcome diminishing returns to research effort, causing AI progress to accelerate further and resulting in an SIE.

records.statement: Davidson and Houlden's paper of August 2025 estimates that a software intelligence explosion would probably (about 60%) compress more than three years of AI progress into less than a year, and is somewhat unlikely (about 20%) to compress more than ten years into less than a year, and calls this an intermediate view.
records.missing: It quantifies a compression of AI progress into under a year but does not state that capability rises to far beyond human level within that period; it places itself between the proposition and its denial.
records.qualification: The authors describe their analysis as speculative and as an 'intermediate view' between 'those who are highly sceptical of intelligence explosion dynamics and those who anticipate extremely rapid and sustained capabilities increases'.

evidence.passage: We think that the software intelligence explosion will probably (~60%) compress >3 years of AI progress into <1 year, but is somewhat unlikely (~20%) to compress >10 years into <1 year.
Our analysis suggests an intermediate view

records.statement: Altman's post of February 2015 states that progress in machine intelligence is a double exponential, that development may look slow and then suddenly go vertical, and that recursive self-improvement makes timelines hard to judge, while allowing that it may be more gradual.
records.missing: It names no period for the rise and uses neither "intelligence explosion" nor a takeoff term; it also allows a gradual course.
records.qualification: The post gives both possibilities ('it also may be more gradual') and names no period.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "It’s very hard to know how close we are"
evidence.passage: Development progress may look relatively slow and then all of a sudden go vertical—things could get out of control very quickly

records.statement: Marcus's paper of January 2018 sets out ten concerns about deep learning, states that it may be approaching a wall, and argues that it must be supplemented by other techniques if artificial general intelligence is to be reached.
records.qualification: The paper argues that deep learning alone is insufficient for general intelligence; it does not address catastrophic risk. Yudkowsky's texts on the overlapping dataset concept Y13 contest that AGI is decades away and are linked.

evidence.passage: I present ten concerns for deep learning, and suggest that deep learning must be supplemented by other techniques if we are to reach artificial general intelligence.
Yet deep learning may well be approaching a wall

records.statement: Marcus's essay of March 2022 argues that the scaling of language models has not delivered genuine comprehension, that deep learning may already be approaching diminishing returns from scale, and that hybrid neurosymbolic AI rather than deep learning alone is the way forward.
records.qualification: The essay is about the route to trustworthy and general AI; it does not discuss catastrophic risk.

evidence.passage: Indeed, we may already be running into scaling limits in deep learning, perhaps already approaching a point of diminishing returns.
hybrid AI, not deep learning alone (nor symbols alone) seems the best way forward

records.statement: Marcus's post of April 2024 reads benchmark results from GPT-2 to GPT-4 Turbo as tentative evidence that large language models have reached a period of diminishing returns, and states that the wall he wrote of in 2022 may be approaching.
records.qualification: The post calls its own plots tentative and discusses the restriction-of-range problem in benchmarks; it is about LLMs, not about catastrophic risk.

evidence.locator: Paragraph after the opening discussion of Mollick
evidence.passage: Instead, I see numerous signs that we have reached a period of diminishing returns.
The wall that I once warned about, in 2022, may finally be approaching.

records.statement: Narayanan and Kapoor's post of June 2024 argues that scaling laws do not predict emergent capabilities, that high-quality training data is running short and model sizes are under downward pressure, and states that there is virtually no chance that scaling alone will lead to AGI.
records.qualification: The post limits its statement to scaling alone and states that how far AI will advance through scaling cannot be predicted exactly.

evidence.passage: While we can't predict exactly how far AI will advance through scaling, we think there’s virtually no chance that scaling alone will lead to AGI.
Every traditional machine learning model eventually plateaus; maybe LLMs are no different.

records.statement: Mitchell's paper of April 2021 describes four fallacies that lead to overconfident predictions about AI, including the assumption that narrow advances lie on a continuum with general intelligence, and states that AI systems remain far from the general abilities that benchmark names suggest.
records.missing: It does not state that current approaches will reach limits short of general intelligence; it argues that predictions of their progress are overconfident.
records.qualification: The paper concerns the reliability of AI predictions and the nature of intelligence; it criticises superintelligence thought experiments by Bostrom and Russell on other grounds.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 4, "Fallacy 1: Narrow intelligence is on a continuum with general intelligence"
evidence.passage: if people see a machine do something amazing, albeit in a narrow area, they often assume the field is that much further along toward general AI.
AI systems are still far from matching the more general human abilities we associate with the benchmarks’ names.

records.statement: Sutton's essay of March 2019 states that the biggest lesson of seventy years of AI research is that general methods that leverage computation, search and learning, are ultimately the most effective by a large margin, because the cost of computation keeps falling.
records.missing: It does not address whether current approaches will reach, or fall short of, general or superhuman intelligence.
records.qualification: The essay is about research method and makes no forecast about general or superhuman AI or about risk.

evidence.passage: general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, and by a large margin.

records.statement: Gwern's essay of 2020 states the scaling hypothesis, on which intelligence is simple neural units and learning algorithms applied to diverse experience at a currently unreachable scale, so that neural networks will become ever more intelligent as computational resources grow.

attested.note: The page dates itself "2020-05-28–2022-01-02", the second date being its stated last modification; the quoted wording is read in the current page, which states no later revision; no earlier copy was compared.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that current neural-network methods will reach limits short of general intelligence.

records.qualification: Read in the current page, which the author dates 2020-05-28 to 2022-01-02; the wording is attested from the later date. The essay states the hypothesis as the author's own expectation, not as demonstrated.

evidence.passage: The scaling hypothesis regards the blessings of scale as the secret of AGI: intelligence is ‘just’ simple neural units & learning algorithms applied to diverse experiences at a (currently) unreachable scale.

records.statement: Altman's essay of September 2024 states that deep learning worked and got predictably better with scale, that the remaining problems will be solved, and that superintelligence may arrive in a few thousand days.

engagement.rationale: It states that gains from scaling will continue, without answering the reasons given for a plateau.

records.qualification: A statement by the chief executive of OpenAI, a developer of the systems in question; it gives no argument against specific arguments for a plateau, and does not address risk.

evidence.passage: In 15 words: deep learning worked, got predictably better with scale, and we dedicated increasing resources to it.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "There are a lot of details"
evidence.passage: Deep learning works, and we will solve the remaining problems.

records.statement: Bengio and twenty-three co-authors' paper of October 2023 states that there is no fundamental reason why AI progress would slow or halt at the human level, noting that AI already surpasses humans in narrow domains and is increasingly used to improve AI systems.

engagement.rationale: It states that there is no fundamental limit at human level, without engaging a named argument for a plateau.

records.qualification: A multi-author consensus paper; the record states what the paper says, not each author's view. Read in arXiv v1; the revised Science version of 2024 was not compared.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 2, opening section, paragraph continuing from p. 1
evidence.passage: There is no fundamental reason why AI progress would slow or halt at the human level.

records.statement: Bengio's post of July 2024 answers the argument that AGI is possible but only in many decades, holding that it cannot be ruled out that AGI is reached by adding some trick to current methods, that capability trend lines continue to point towards AGI, and that regulation takes years to put in place.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that current methods are known to fall short of AGI for decades.

records.qualification: Bengio agrees that current systems show gaps that may require new breakthroughs; his argument concerns uncertainty about timing and the time needed for regulation, not a forecast that AGI is near.

evidence.locator: Section "For those who think AGI is possible but only in many decades"
evidence.passage: First, it is impossible to be sure that AGI will not be achieved by adding some trick on top of current methods, and the capability trend lines continue to point towards AGI.

records.statement: Yudkowsky's reply of December 2017 to Chollet's essay argues that Chollet's arguments do not establish that recursive intelligence expansion progresses at a roughly linear pace, and that even Hanson would reject the idea that progress within all systems is confined to such a pace.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise, quoted from Chollet, that recursive intelligence expansion is confined to a roughly linear pace.

records.qualification: The reply addresses the validity of Chollet's arguments and states that it does not try to make the whole case for an intelligence explosion; Chollet's essay is quoted in the reply but was not retrieved.

evidence.locator: Closing section, after the quotation on "a roughly linear pace"
evidence.passage: If this were to be true, I don’t think it would be established by the arguments given.
I expect that even Robin Hanson, who was broadly opposing my side of this debate, would have a coughing fit over the idea that progress within all systems is confined to a roughly linear pace.

replies.statement: Yudkowsky's post of 6 December 2017 replies to Chollet's essay "The impossibility of intelligence explosion", which it names.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other.

evidence.passage: This is a reply to Francois Chollet, the inventor of the Keras wrapper for the Tensorflow and Theano deep learning systems, on his essay “The impossibility of intelligence explosion.”

replies.statement: Thorstad's working paper of November 2022 replies to Chalmers's paper of 2010, which it names and discusses in its Section 4.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 3, Introduction, plan of the paper
evidence.passage: Sections 4-5 consider recent philosophical arguments for the singularity hypothesis by Chalmers (2010) and Bostrom (2014), showing how these arguments fail to support the hypothesis’ growth assumptions.

replies.statement: Narayanan and Kapoor's post of June 2024 addresses Aschenbrenner's essay of 2024, which it names, in its further-reading note.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other.

evidence.passage: A recent essay by Leopold Aschenbrenner made waves due to its claim that “AGI by 2027 is strikingly plausible”. We haven’t tried to give a point-by-point rebuttal here
His arguments for his timeline are entertaining and thought provoking, but fundamentally an exercise in trendline extrapolation.

debates.title: Chollet and Yudkowsky on intelligence explosion, 2017
debates.note: Yudkowsky's reply on the MIRI blog quotes Chollet's essay passage by passage. Chollet's essay (Medium) refused retrieval (HTTP 403), so his side rests on no record here; the passages quoted in the reply are a relay and were not used as evidence of Chollet's text.

debates.title: Thorstad's reply to Chalmers on the singularity hypothesis
debates.note: One-way exchange located: Thorstad's working paper answers Chalmers (2010). Hutter, 'Can Intelligence Explode?' (arXiv 2012), also answers Chalmers but is not recorded (see omissions). A reply by Chalmers was not searched for.

debates.title: Aschenbrenner and Narayanan–Kapoor on scaling to AGI, 2024
debates.note: Narayanan and Kapoor's post names Aschenbrenner's essay and states that most of the post was drafted before it appeared; it is not a point-by-point reply.

debates.title: Hanson–Yudkowsky AI-foom debate and later posts, 2008–2022
debates.note: The debate of 2008–2013 is in the dataset and is linked, not re-recorded. The pack adds later posts by the two participants: Hanson (2014, 2022) and Yudkowsky (2017), which names 'my and Robin Hanson’s AI-foom debate'. No reply item is made for Yudkowsky's post because it names the debate rather than one text; Hanson's reply to it on LessWrong, linked from the MIRI page as 'Reply from Robin Hanson', could not be retrieved (HTTP 403).

debates.title: Christiano and Yudkowsky on takeoff speeds, 2018–2022
debates.note: In the dataset (A4, Y11) and linked; the pack adds only a record of Christiano (2018) on R16.

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: Chalmers (2010, dataset copy), Kelly (2017), Brooks (2017), AI Impacts (2018) and Grace (2022), Drexler (2019), Aschenbrenner (2024), AI 2027 (2025), Narayanan and Kapoor (2025), Hanson's posts after 2013 (2014, 2019, 2022), Yudkowsky's MIRI posts of 2017. Chollet (2017) refused retrieval. Davidson's compute-centric takeoff report (2023) refused retrieval at Open Philanthropy and the Alignment Forum; his Forethought papers of 2025 (with Eth; with Houlden) were read instead. Bostrom (2002, 2003) read from caches shared with other groups. arXiv API, all fields, sorted by submission date ascending, first 50 results read by title and abstract: "intelligence explosion" (16 results), "fast takeoff" OR "hard takeoff" OR "slow takeoff" (1), "recursive self-improvement" (224; first 50), title "technological singularity" (10); read in full: Walsh 2016, Benthall 2017, Hutter 2012, Yampolskiy 2015, Sarma 2017, Whitfill and Wu 2025, MacAskill and Moorhouse 2025. Thorstad (2022) and Muehlhauser and Salamon (2012) located by web search for discovery and read in their primary PDFs. Web search used for discovery only (Hanson's post address).
searchLog.earliestNote: Bostrom (2003) meets the criterion (a transition from roughly human-level AI to superintelligence 'perhaps a matter of days rather than years') but is read only in an undated revised copy, so it does not hold the earliest-located role. Yudkowsky (20 October 2017) holds it, and meets the criterion only through the name “foom”, not through a stated period. Chalmers (2010) and Muehlhauser and Salamon (2012) are recorded as bearing on it, since neither states a period of hours to months. Bostrom (2002) was read and found to state a sudden transition only for uploads, conditionally. On the overlapping dataset concepts A4/A1, Yudkowsky's Creating Friendly AI (2001) and AI as a Positive and Negative Factor in Global Risk (2006) precede it in the period, and Good (1965) and Vinge (1993) precede the period; they are linked, not re-recorded. The earliest located contesting record within the pack is Hanson (2014); Hanson's What Core Argument? (2008) contests A4 in the dataset.

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: Marcus (2018, arXiv v1; 2022, Nautilus), Mitchell (2021, arXiv v1), Sutton (2019). Further texts located from the seed texts and by web search for discovery: Marcus (2024), Narayanan and Kapoor, 'AI scaling myths' (2024), Aschenbrenner (2024, chapter I), Gwern, 'The Scaling Hypothesis' (2020), Altman, 'The Intelligence Age' (2024), Bengio et al. (2023, arXiv v1) and Bengio (2024). No arXiv API search was run for R13's usual names ('hitting a wall', 'plateau', 'diminishing returns'), whose results would be dominated by technical papers on training dynamics; this is a gap.
searchLog.earliestNote: Marcus (2018) is the earliest text found that states that deep learning alone will not reach general intelligence. The dataset's Y13 records (Yudkowsky, 2000–2021) contest or bear on 'AGI is decades away' and are linked. Earlier statements that some approach to AI would fall short (Dreyfus, 1972, and others before 2000) are outside the period; Brooks (2017), Kelly (2017) and Walsh (2016) make related claims about distance to AGI but not about the limits of current approaches and were recorded on R05 or R16 instead. Earliest contesting located: Gwern, The Scaling Hypothesis (page dated 2020-05-28 to 2022-01-02; wording attested from 2022-01-02).

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: Christiano (2018, dataset address), Brooks (2017), Narayanan and Kapoor (2025), Drexler (2019), AI Impacts (2018), Grace (2022), Hanson (2014, 2022). Contesting texts located from the replies: Yudkowsky (2017, two posts). Kokotajlo, 'Against GDP as a metric for timelines and takeoff speeds' (LessWrong, 2020), and Davidson's takeoff report (2023) could not be retrieved.
searchLog.earliestNote: Brooks (September 2017) is the earliest articulation found; Christiano (February 2018) follows. The dataset's Y11 records (Yudkowsky, from 2000) are contesting or context records on a related concept, so no earlier articulation is linked. Hanson's posts (2008–2014) argue against a local explosion rather than stating a gradual transition in the criterion's terms; Hanson (2014) is recorded as contesting R05. The two contesting records are both Yudkowsky's, which leaves the risk side of R16 thin; the search found no other text that explicitly argues against a gradual takeoff.

searchLog.searched: Count by position: risk side (articulating R05, contesting R13 or R16) 15 records; counter side (contesting R05, articulating R13 or R16) 17 records; bears_on 4 (two on R05, two on R13). The group paragraph asked for about 40 records; 36 were made, because three seed texts refused retrieval (Chollet 2017, Davidson 2023, Kokotajlo 2020) and several arXiv results were found not to meet the criteria.

openQuestions.question: R05 overlaps A4/A1. Should these records be admitted onto A4 (fast or hard takeoff) and A1 (intelligence explosion) or onto a concept of their own?
openQuestions.recommended: Admit onto A4 as the overlap note recommends, keeping the earliest-located role scoped to texts outside the dataset's A4 records, since Creating Friendly AI (2001) already precedes Bostrom (2003) on A4.

openQuestions.question: Several documents may be defined by more than one group: bostrom-2003-ethical-issues (goals-and-drives), altman-2015-machine-intelligence-part-1 (catastrophe-and-priorities), bengio-2023-managing-extreme-risks and bengio-2024-reasoning-arguments (catastrophe-and-priorities), narayanan-kapoor and Aschenbrenner texts (openness-and-incentives).
openQuestions.recommended: Reconcile ids and documentWords at merge; this draft uses the other groups' document ids and cache keys where they were visible, and its own cache key for the Bengio et al. arXiv v1.

openQuestions.question: The R13 criterion joins a claim about limits of current approaches with the consequence that catastrophe-capable AI is not near; Marcus (2018, 2022) and Narayanan and Kapoor (2024) state the first part only.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep them as articulations with qualifications, or reword the criterion so that the second clause is a consequence rather than a requirement. Resolved on 2026-10-29: the consequence clause was removed from the R13 criterion.
